title: Designing Google Maps

facts.text: As of March 2021 Google Maps had one billion daily active users and 99% coverage of the world; the simplified design breaks into 3 high-level components.
The location service records user location updates, which clients send every few seconds.
Location data is used to detect new and recently closed roads, to improve the map's accuracy over time, and as an input for live traffic data.
For map rendering, the world's map is projected into a huge 2D image and broken into small blocks called tiles.
Tiles are static and rarely change, so an efficient way to serve them is a CDN backed by cloud storage such as S3, with users loading the tiles they need from a nearby CDN.
To support zooming and panning, pre-calculate the map blocks at different zoom levels and load the images when needed.
The navigation service finds a reasonably fast route from point A to point B, calling a Geocoding Service to resolve an address to a latitude/longitude pair and a Route Planner Service.

The Route Planner calculates the top-K shortest paths between A and B, estimates the time of each path from current traffic and historical data, then ranks the paths by predicted time and user filtering.

notes: thin: the guide is a short overview of three components. It has no requirements, storage estimates, road-graph data model, routing algorithm detail, ETA or traffic pipeline, or API. The toll example sentence (bcd4187fdc2f) reads 'the user doesn't want to avoid tolls', probably a typo for 'wants to avoid'; the fact therefore says only 'user filtering'.

title: Map tiles

definition.text: A world map projected into one huge 2D image and cut into small static image blocks that clients load to compose the visible map.

facts.text: The world's map is projected into a huge 2D image and broken down into small image blocks called tiles.
Tiles are static and do not change very often, so a CDN backed by cloud storage like S3 serves them efficiently, and users load the tiles they need from a nearby CDN.
For zooming and panning, the map blocks are pre-calculated at different zoom levels and the images are loaded when needed.

notes: thin: only one short guide section describes tiles; no source gives tile sizes, numbering or projection details.
